beats.say: K-means asks for a number of groups. Choose three centers here, with one seed in each visible area. Hold them still. Compare each point with the centers and connect it to the nearest one. The colors now record assignments, rather than supplied topic labels.

Keep those memberships fixed. Where should the left center move? Average its two horizontal coordinates, then its two vertical coordinates. That midpoint minimizes the sum of squared distances to these members. Move all three centers to their own means and watch the objective fall.

Assign again around the new centers. The same pairs remain, so this run has settled. Lloyd's algorithm alternates these two steps. Exact assignments and means preserve or reduce inertia. Different seeds can find different solutions; compare restarts, and repair an empty group before averaging it.

Return to the duplicate-charge query. An inverted-file index stores each message under its nearest center. Compare the query with our three centers. The upper center is just closer than the left center. Before opening a list, predict which reply that shortcut will return.

Open only the upper list and compare its two messages. The best candidate is the reset-link message. Now check all six documents as a flat-search reference. The duplicate-payment message is actually nearer. Its center was farther away, so the one-list shortcut hid the right candidate.

Probe the next cell as well. The duplicate-payment message enters the candidate set and wins. That recovers the exact neighbor for this query. Count three center comparisons plus four document comparisons: seven, versus six for flat search. Larger corpora can benefit; measure candidate work, latency and recall together.

Try one new stress test. This separate collection has wide horizontal variation, with three documents stacked near the middle. A user asks why their sign-in code fails. In full space, the login document is closest. One principal component keeps almost ninety-eight percent of the corpus variance. Would you trust that shortcut?

Keep the horizontal component and project the query too. The login document, billing help and runbook note all land on zero. Their distances to the compressed query tie. The quiet vertical direction carried the distinction this question needed. A first-match implementation can now return the wrong reply.

Restore the second component. The login document separates from the alternatives and becomes the unique nearest neighbor again. Our two shortcuts changed different things: clusters restricted candidates, while projection removed coordinates. Evaluate both against the original search and reviewed query-answer pairs before choosing the smaller representation.

Keep only the first score. Reconstruct C by stepping along that direction, then adding the fitted mean back. The gap to the original is perpendicular. Square its length. Repeat for all six points: these discarded residuals account for the spread that one component leaves behind.

This projection keeps about eighty-five percent of total variance. Add the second perpendicular component and every point returns to its original position, with zero reconstruction error. The Pythagorean split connects maximum retained spread with minimum squared residual. Retrieval still needs its own test.
